Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Vignette:
Vincent is a fifty-eight-year-old hairdresser who has been married for thirty-two years. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he is not entirely sure what talking can do now. The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, outside the barbershop where he had worked for two decades. He was closing up late on a Thursday evening, a cool September night, when a man stepped out from beside the dumpster and pressed something hard into Vincent’s ribs. The man smelled sharply of alcohol, and that smell—cheap whiskey layered over sweat—is now a scent Vincent cannot separate from the cold pressure of what he believed was a gun against his body. The man demanded his wallet and his phone. Vincent handed them over without a word, his hands shaking so badly he dropped the wallet twice. The man ran off into the alley, and Vincent stood there for what felt like a long time, unable to move, unable to speak, his heart pounding so hard he thought he might be having a heart attack.

In the months that followed, Vincent found that the event would not stay in the past. It came back to him in vivid pictures—the glint of the streetlight on the man’s eyes, the brick wall beside the dumpster, the angle of the man’s hand. These images arrived without warning, like a film that played over and over, always the same sequence, always ending with that moment of frozen silence. He knew exactly what had happened, could see it clearly, yet when his wife asked him to describe the robbery, he found himself unable to form the words. The images were there, sharp and relentless, but the sentences to explain them would not come.

Vincent began to avoid people. At first it was subtle—he stopped walking to the corner store for lunch, started eating alone in the back of the shop. Then he began turning down invitations from his colleagues, stopped attending the monthly staff meetings that had once been a source of camaraderie. He told himself it was because people acted suspiciously now. He had come to believe that anyone who moved too quickly, anyone who looked at him twice, anyone who stood too close—they were all potential threats. He found himself scanning every customer who came into the salon, watching their hands, their eyes, the way they stood. What frightened him most was that he could not tell the difference between a genuine threat and an ordinary person anymore. Everyone seemed dangerous.

The avoidance brought consequences. His regular clients began to notice that he was distracted, that he flinched when they touched his shoulder, that he seemed to be somewhere else. One longtime client, Mrs. Delgado, corrected him gently when he started shampooing her hair before cutting it, and Vincent felt a surge of something he could not name—shame, perhaps, or anger. He began to dwell on what he had done wrong. He replayed the night of the robbery and asked himself why he had not fought back, why he had not run, why he had not noticed the man sooner. He applied the same scrutiny to every interaction: when a customer asked him to redo a trim, he spent hours afterward turning over what he had done to deserve the criticism. He was certain that he was missing something, that people could see his weakness, that he was failing in ways he could not fully grasp.

He tried hard not to think about the robbery. He told himself it was over, that he was fine, that he needed to move on. But the harder he pushed the memories away, the more forcefully they returned—those same images, that same film, playing at the worst possible moments. When a young man came into the shop smelling of beer, Vincent’s hands went cold and he had to excuse himself to the back room. He stood there, gripping the counter, trying to breathe, knowing that the smell was just a smell, that the customer was just a customer, but unable to make his body believe it.

What finally brought Vincent to therapy was a moment in the salon last week. A new client, a woman in her thirties, asked him a simple question about the price of a haircut, and Vincent found himself unable to answer. His mouth opened but no words came out. He stood there, frozen, the image of the robber’s hand pressing into his ribs flashing behind his eyes. The woman looked at him with concern, and Vincent had to walk away. He went home early that day and told his wife that he could not keep doing this. He is afraid that he is losing his ability to work, to speak, to be himself. What he hopes for, though he cannot quite say it, is that someone might help him find the words that have been lost to him.
